title: Capacity of the binary deletion channel
formal:
Supply a function \(g:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) and prove
\[\forall\delta\in[0,1],\quad |g(\delta)-C(\delta)|\le\frac1{100},\]
where \(C(\delta)\) is the operational capacity of the binary independent deletion channel, measured in bits per input bit. The probability \(\delta\) is fixed as the block length tends to infinity. This retained benchmark is a formalization task at the stated accuracy: an unrestricted finite approximation scheme is already known. It does not require a new exact capacity formula.
definitions:
Channel. For each positive integer \(n\), an input is a binary string \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Independently at each of its \(n\) positions, the channel deletes the bit with probability \(\delta\) and retains it with probability \(1-\delta\). It outputs the retained bits in their original order. The output alphabet is the disjoint union \(\mathcal Y_n=\bigcup_{k=0}^n\{0,1\}^k\), including the empty string. The receiver observes the string and its length, but neither terminal observes the deletion positions. There are no erasure markers, insertions, substitutions, feedback or additional communication channels. Both terminals know \(n\) and the real parameter \(\delta\).

Transition probabilities. For \(y\in\{0,1\}^k\) with \(0\le k\le n\), let \(e_x(y)\) be the number of increasing tuples \(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_k\le n\) such that \(x_{i_j}=y_j\) for all \(j\). The empty tuple has count one. Then
\[\mu_{n,\delta}(y\mid x)=e_x(y)(1-\delta)^k\delta^{n-k}.\]
Use \(0^0=1\) in this finite probability formula, so it also defines both endpoints. Distinct deletion patterns producing the same string contribute separately; repeated symbols do not identify their original positions.

Codes and error. A length-\(n\) code has a positive integer message count \(M_n\) and deterministic maps
\[\operatorname{Enc}_n:[M_n]\to\{0,1\}^n,\qquad \operatorname{Dec}_n:\mathcal Y_n\to[M_n],\]
where \([M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}\). A uniformly distributed message is encoded once and sent through the channel. Average error is
\[P_{e,n}=\frac1{M_n}\sum_{m=1}^{M_n}\sum_{y\in\mathcal Y_n}\mu_{n,\delta}(y\mid\operatorname{Enc}_n(m))\,\mathbf1\{\operatorname{Dec}_n(y)\ne m\}.\]
The encoder need not be injective by definition; the reliability condition still applies to every message in this average. Any repetition, redundancy or markers inserted by the encoder are part of its \(n\) transmitted bits and are charged in the rate. There is no shared randomness or state supplied outside this code. Encoding and decoding have no time or storage bounds. Their maps may depend arbitrarily on \(n\) and the known \(\delta\); a uniform algorithm producing the family is not required.

Achievable rate and capacity. For a fixed \(\delta\), a real rate \(R\ge0\) is achievable if codes exist for every positive integer \(n\) with
\[P_{e,n}\longrightarrow0,\qquad \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{\log_2 M_n}{n}\ge R.\]
Define \(C(\delta)\) as the supremum of all achievable nonnegative rates. It is not assumed that a code family attains this supremum. The denominator is the number of input bits, not the random number of surviving bits. The noiseless and completely deleted endpoints give \(C(0)=1\) and \(C(1)=0\), and \(0\le C(\delta)\le1-\delta\) throughout the domain.

Finite-block information. For a probability distribution \(P\) on a finite set, write \(H(P)=-\sum_{z:P(z)>0}P(z)\log_2 P(z)\). If \(p\) is a distribution on \(\{0,1\}^n\), let \(q(y)=\sum_x p(x)\mu_{n,\delta}(y\mid x)\) and define
\[I_p(X;Y)=H(q)-\sum_x p(x)H(\mu_{n,\delta}(\,\cdot\mid x)),\qquad C_n(\delta)=\frac1n\max_p I_p(X;Y).\]
The maximum ranges over all probability distributions on the finite input alphabet, including correlated input bits, and exists by compactness and continuity. The coding theorem identifies \(C(\delta)=\lim_{n\to\infty}C_n(\delta)\). These \(C_n\) are normalized per input bit; some references instead use the same symbol for the unnormalized maximum.
answer_criterion:
Give an unambiguous real-valued function on the entire real interval \([0,1]\) and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated absolute-error inequality, with the operational capacity and channel defined above. A formula, a certified evaluation rule or another mathematical description may specify the answer. No polynomial evaluation-time bound, prescribed expression grammar, numerical table size or new scientific theorem is required. An exact determination also qualifies.

A pair of functions \(L,U\) with proved inequalities \(L(\delta)\le C(\delta)\le U(\delta)\) and \(U(\delta)-L(\delta)\le1/50\) for every \(\delta\) qualifies through its midpoint. The proof must establish the full real-parameter domain and both coding and converse sides needed for the certificate. If it uses an information-theoretic characterization instead of the operational definition, their equivalence must be part of the checked justification. Merely renaming the defining capacity, restating an unevaluated asymptotic limit without a proved error bound, giving an uncertified plot, or checking finitely many parameter values is insufficient.

This is deliberately a formalization benchmark for a known approximation guarantee. A rigorous finite-block description with a proved uniform error bound can qualify even if its practical evaluation is prohibitive. It need not improve known numerical bounds or settle the separate exact-capacity question.
why: The binary deletion channel isolates the information cost of hidden synchronization errors. Its exact capacity curve remains a central coding question. This user-retained approximation task instead tests an end-to-end Lean formalization connecting reliable transmission to a certified finite description of the capacity curve.

importance.reason: The canonical capacity problem for synchronization errors, connecting coding, information theory, sequence reconstruction and the structure of optimal input processes.

progress.text: Dobrushin establishes a coding theorem relating operational capacity of synchronization channels to normalized multiletter mutual information.

Dalai records a uniform finite-block bracket of width \(\log_2(n+1)/n\) for all deletion probabilities. Unrestricted fixed-accuracy approximation is therefore known; the retained Lean task formalizes this type of guarantee.
Kanoria–Montanari determine the small-deletion expansion through the \(\delta ^{2}\) term and input processes achieving that order.
Rubinstein–Con improve run-based achievable rates and finite-channel numerical converses; their universal lower bound is \(0.1221(1- \delta )\).
Pinto–Ribeiro improve computer-assisted upper bounds, including \(0.3578(1- \delta )\) for \(\delta \ge 0.64\) and a reported 0.1896 upper bound at \(\delta =1/2\).
Chen posts a claimed certified lower bound \(C(1/2)>0.11032415\). The preprint and its limits are recorded; the numerical certificate is not independently reproduced in this review.

Soysal claims the upper bound \((1-\delta)/4\) for \(13/20\le\delta<1\), with finite-block converses and an author-reported Lean verification. The external proof and certificate were not independently replayed in this review.

status_note: Checked on 16 September 2026. The exact binary deletion-channel capacity curve remains open in the inspected primary sources. The retained absolute 1/100 approximation guarantee is already available in principle from the classical uniform finite-block bound; the user explicitly retains it as a Lean formalization task, not a claim of unresolved approximate capacity. The August half-deletion and September high-deletion improvements are recorded as claims whose certificates were not independently rerun. Neither claims an exact full-curve resolution.

context_blocks.text: A deletion removes a bit and also hides where it belonged. For example, receiving 00 after sending three bits is compatible with several input strings and deletion patterns. The output length reveals how many symbols survived, but it does not reveal their positions. This uncertainty couples the interpretation of consecutive output symbols even though the deletion decisions themselves are independent.

If the receiver were additionally given the deletion locations, the channel would become the binary erasure channel with capacity \(1- \delta\). Revealing information cannot make decoding harder, so \(C(\delta )\le 1- \delta\) is an immediate upper bound. The challenge is to quantify the further loss caused by missing alignment. Counting surviving bits alone therefore does not determine the answer.

The approximation guarantee is already a classical result. Dalai’s Lemma 1 states, for every \(n\ge1\) and every \(\delta\in[0,1]\),
\[C_n(\delta)-\frac{\log_2(n+1)}n\le C(\delta)\le C_n(\delta).\]
The error bound is independent of the deletion probability and tends to zero. It therefore yields fixed-accuracy determination in principle, despite the \(2^n\)-element input alphabet. There is no unresolved existence of an unrestricted approximation scheme at the retained tolerance. The user explicitly chose to keep its complete Lean formalization as this card’s benchmark.

The input bits in a code need not be independent, and restricting the optimizing distributions would change the capacity problem. Rubinstein and Con prove \(C(\delta)>0.1221(1-\delta)\) for every \(0<\delta<1\). Their result establishes a positive constant fraction of the surviving-bit rate throughout the open interval. It is a lower bound on the unrestricted capacity, not an equality or a requirement that every optimal code use their particular input process.

Near the noiseless endpoint, a much sharper asymptotic description is available. Kanoria and Montanari prove \(C(\delta )=1+\delta  \log _{2} \delta - A_{1}\delta +A_{2}\delta ^{2}+O(\delta ^{3- \varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) as \(\delta\) tends to zero, with explicit constants \(A_{1}\approx 1.15416377\) and \(A_{2}\approx 1.67814594\). They also identify input distributions achieving this order. This determines several leading terms, but its remainder does not vanish identically at a fixed nonzero deletion probability.

Numerical converse bounds use finite channels in which the input and output lengths are bounded and the transition matrix is explicit. Blahut–Arimoto optimization can bound their capacities, which in turn upper-bound the unsegmented deletion channel. Pinto and Ribeiro’s 2026 implementation handles larger instances, including selected input lengths of 31, and reports \(C(\delta )\le 0.3578(1- \delta )\) for \(\delta \ge 0.64\). These are computer-assisted bounds reported by the authors; this review has not rerun their large computations.

Published numerical estimates still leave a substantial practical gap at half deletion: the 2023 table gives an achievable rate above 0.104075, and the April 2026 upper-bound table reports 0.1896. These particular computations do not certify the full curve to absolute error 0.01. This practical gap is consistent with the classical finite approximation theorem: the latter imposes no feasible computation limit and may require an enormous finite optimization.

An August 2026 preprint by Chen claims a further half-deletion lower bound above 0.11032415, using joint information from several output runs and a rational certificate. Its asserted slightly sharper upper number is conditional on a precision assumption about a previously published table. This card records the new lower bound as a preprint claim whose certificate has not been independently reproduced here, and does not present the conditional upper number as a separately established converse. Even if the new lower bound is confirmed, a substantial gap remains.

A September 2026 preprint by Soysal claims
\[C(\delta)\le\frac{1-\delta}{4}\qquad\text{for }\frac{13}{20}\le\delta<1,\]
together with finite-block information and decoding-error bounds. The paper supplies a Lean development and exact finite certificate. Its repository reports separate fresh replay of the components followed by checking final theorems over those verified imports. This review inspected the theorem statements, verification description and author’s machine-readable record; it did not rerun the large proof. The claim concerns a one-sided bound on only part of the domain, and does not determine the exact curve or supply the entire accuracy certificate in this card.

This is a transmission problem: the sender may select a codebook designed for the channel. Trace reconstruction instead starts with an arbitrary unknown string and observes repeated independently deleted copies of that same string. Adversarial deletion codes also use a different error model. Progress in either neighboring subject can be informative without giving the capacity curve with the certified accuracy required here.
